replacement: “I tell you, I’m waiting for news, priceless news, and so I don’t want Mitya at all. And I feel that he didn’t believe I’d stay at Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. He must be lying in ambush now, in the garden behind Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, watching for me. And if he’s there, he won’t come here, which is all the better! But I really did go to Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. Mitya took me there himself. I told him I’d stay till midnight, and I asked him to be sure to come at midnight and take me home. He left, and I sat ten minutes with Kuzma Kuzmitch and came back here. Ugh, I was scared. I ran, so as not to bump into him.”

Alyosha said nothing. He sat there afraid to move. He heard her words, “Tell me, and I’ll get off,” but he did not answer. Still, nothing stirred in his heart of what Rakitin, say, watching him spitefully from his corner, might have expected or imagined. His great grief swallowed every feeling that might have been roused. If he had been able to think clearly just then, he would have seen that he was wearing the strongest armor against every lust and temptation. Yet, dazed as he was and crushed by sorrow, he could not help noticing a new and strange feeling in his heart. This woman, this “dreadful” woman, did not frighten him now. He felt none of the fear that used to rise in his soul whenever a thought of any woman crossed his mind. Quite the opposite. This was the woman he had feared more than any other, and she was sitting on his knee with her arms around him. She woke in him a different, unexpected, odd feeling: the keenest, purest interest, with no trace of his old terror. That was what instinctively surprised him.

“Does he know! Of course not. If he knew, there’d be murder. But I’m not afraid of that now, I’m not afraid of his knife. Quiet, Rakitin, don’t remind me of Dmitri Fyodorovitch. He’s bruised my heart. I don’t want to think about that right now. I can think about Alyosha, I can look at Alyosha ... smile at me, dear, cheer up, smile at my silliness, at my happiness.... Ah, he’s smiling, he’s smiling! How kindly he looks at me! And you know, Alyosha, all this time I’ve been thinking you were angry with me about the day before yesterday, about that young lady. I behaved like a cur, that’s the truth.... But it’s good that it happened. It was horrid, but good as well.” Grushenka smiled dreamily, and a faintly cruel line showed in her smile. “Mitya told me she screamed that I ‘ought to be flogged.’ I did insult her terribly. She sent for me, she wanted to make a conquest of me, to win me over with her chocolate.... No, it’s good that it ended like that.” She smiled again. “But I’m still afraid you’re angry with me.”
“That’s a woman’s way of looking at it!”

“How touching and sentimental!” said Rakitin with a sneer. “And she’s sitting on his knee, too! He has something to grieve over, but what’s the matter with you? He’s rebelling against his God and ready to eat sausage....”
